title: The daily routine
teaches: Run the trading day on three checkpoints: a premarket that reads the futures, the calendar and the news, then narrows the list to a few names with levels, entries, stops and alerts; a midday check on what you hold, your stops and news due later; and a recap after the close that reviews stops, checks tonight's reports and writes tomorrow's plan.

walkthroughs.title: Before the open
steps: Run the day on three checkpoints: before the open, during the session, and after the close.
Start wide. Index futures trade nearly 24 hours, so they show how the market took the overnight news.
Then the calendar. CPI lands at 8:30 a.m. ET, and companies usually report before the open or after the close.
Then narrow your list to the few best names. Each gets levels, an entry, a stop and a risk amount.

walkthroughs.title: During the session
steps: Volume is usually heavy early, slows at midday, and picks up again into the close.
Midday is a check, not a hunt: what you own, your stops, and news due later, like a 2:00 p.m. Fed statement.
The rules you wrote stay the rules. Changes wait until the market is closed.

walkthroughs.title: After the close
steps: The recap starts with what you own. Check each stop, and consider raising it under a new higher low.
Check who reports tonight or before tomorrow's open. News after the close can gap a stock past your stop.
Then log today's ideas and write tomorrow's list and levels while the market is closed.
Veteran trader Gatis Roze found his best planned days generally gave his best results.

questions.q: Before the 9:30 a.m. ET open, what do S&P 500 futures show you?
choices: How the market takes overnight news
The exact price stocks will open at
Which stocks will lead today
Nothing that matters for stocks
questions.answer: How the market takes overnight news
questions.why: How the market takes overnight news. The futures trade nearly 24 hours, so they react while the regular session is closed. SPY's premarket quotes move with them.
questions.lesson_line: Futures are the market's overnight vote. A hint about the open, not a promise.

wrong.The exact price stocks will open at: No. The open is set by supply and demand at the open itself, and premarket prices may not hold.
wrong.Which stocks will lead today: The futures track the whole index. They can't tell you which names will lead.
wrong.Nothing that matters for stocks: They do matter. SPY's premarket quotes move with the futures, and a big gap moves the largest index stocks too.

questions.q: Midday is usually the busiest, most volatile stretch of the trading day.
questions.why: False. Volume is heavy early, often slows at midday, and grows again into the close. The middle of the day tends to be the calmest stretch.
questions.lesson_line: Busy open, quiet middle, busy close. Plan your checks around that shape.

questions.q: You're building tomorrow's watchlist. What earns a stock a spot on it?
choices: It meets your setup criteria
It was today's biggest gainer
A chat room is buzzing about it
questions.why: It meets your setup criteria. A watchlist holds the names that fit your rules, so you can watch them for an entry signal.
questions.lesson_line: The list is for names that fit your setups, not names that are loud.

wrong.It was today's biggest gainer: A big day can be part of a setup, but on its own it's just a move. The list holds names that meet your criteria.
wrong.A chat room is buzzing about it: Buzz isn't a criterion. Investopedia warns that many chat-room posters have ulterior motives. Check the name against your own rules.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The economic ___ lists the scheduled reports and events that can move the whole market.
questions.why: Calendar. The economic calendar lists the scheduled dates of big reports and events that can move a stock or the whole market. BLS, for one, posts its release dates and times in Eastern Time.
questions.lesson_line: Check the economic calendar every premarket. A scheduled report can move the whole market.

questions.q: Your levels are marked on four names. How do you catch the moment one of them trades?
choices: Set price alerts at your levels
Keep flipping through the charts
Buy all four now so none get away
questions.answer: Set price alerts at your levels
questions.why: Set price alerts at your levels. SMB trader Steve Spencer loads alerts at key prices before the open, so the market tells him when a level trades.
questions.lesson_line: Let alerts do the watching. You show up when a level trades.

wrong.Keep flipping through the charts: You'll catch some levels and miss others, and constant flipping invites impulse trades.
wrong.Buy all four now so none get away: That skips your entry rules. Rules set before you buy are what take the guesswork out of the entry.

questions.q: Once the bell rings, it's fine to rewrite your entry and stop rules on the fly.
questions.why: False. Your rules shouldn't change while you're trading. Rework them when the market is closed, not as a knee-jerk reaction mid-session.
questions.lesson_line: During the session you execute. Rule changes wait for the close.

questions.q: Your scan found a perfect-looking chart. What else does your premarket check before you plan the buy?
choices: The market's trend and its sector
Nothing, a great chart is enough
Analysts' price targets for it
questions.answer: The market's trend and its sector
questions.why: The market's trend and its sector. CAN SLIM checks market direction daily, and leaders usually come from leading groups. Veteran trader Gatis Roze finds a stock rarely rises apart from its sector.
questions.lesson_line: Read the market and the group, then the stock.

wrong.Nothing, a great chart is enough: Charts don't trade in a vacuum. You do better trading in the direction of the bigger trend.
wrong.Analysts' price targets for it: A target is someone's opinion about where it could go. It doesn't tell you if the market is helping or hurting right now.

questions.story: CPI morning. The report is due at 8:30 a.m. ET. At 8:00 your plan is set: three names, with levels, entries and stops.
questions.q: What do you do when the number hits?
choices: See how the market takes it, then adjust
Ignore it, CPI doesn't move stocks
Scrap the plan and start over
Buy all three before it comes out
questions.answer: See how the market takes it, then adjust
questions.why: See how the market takes it, then adjust. CPI can move the whole market, and the futures react before stocks open at 9:30. Trading coach Brett Steenbarger adjusts his game plan as reports come out and markets respond.
questions.lesson_line: Know the calendar before you plan. A scheduled report can rewrite the morning.

wrong.Ignore it, CPI doesn't move stocks: It does. CME lists CPI and the jobs report among the economic reports that move markets.
wrong.Scrap the plan and start over: The plan is a draft, not trash. Steenbarger adjusts his game plan as the reports come out.
wrong.Buy all three before it comes out: That bets on a number nobody has seen yet, in a thin premarket with little price competition.

questions.q: S&P 500 futures were at 6,000 at 4:00 p.m. yesterday. At 8:45 a.m. today they're at 5,940. How far down are they, in percent?
questions.why: 1%. From 6,000 to 5,940 is a 1% drop. The futures track the S&P 500, and SPY and the biggest index stocks tend to move with them before the open.
questions.lesson_line: Read futures in percent, not points. Points mean little until you size them against the level.

questions.q: Before the open you mark yesterday's high, low and close on a name. Which one is our default stop for a new long?
choices: Yesterday's low
Yesterday's high
Yesterday's close
questions.why: Yesterday's low. Our default stop is the low of the day or the prior day's low. Before the open, today's low doesn't exist yet, so yesterday's low is the one you can mark.
questions.lesson_line: Mark yesterday's high and low on every name. Our default stop sits under a low.

wrong.Yesterday's high: Worth marking, but our default stop for a long sits under a low, not at a high.
wrong.Yesterday's close: Useful context, but our default stop uses the low of the day or the prior day's low, not the close.

questions.story: Sunday night your scans leave 45 names. Monday you get 20 minutes of prep before work.
questions.q: What do you do with the list tonight?
choices: Narrow it to the few best setups
Watch all 45 and react to movers
Buy a little of each to be safe
Add names so you miss nothing
questions.answer: Narrow it to the few best setups
questions.why: Narrow it to the few best setups. Twenty minutes won't cover 45 charts well. As trading coach Brett Steenbarger notes, ranking ideas during prep is what lets you act fast when one sets up.
questions.lesson_line: Narrow your list. The best names get your attention, the rest wait.

wrong.Watch all 45 and react to movers: That's more than you can follow closely, and reacting to movers turns into chasing them.
wrong.Buy a little of each to be safe: That's dozens of trades with no plan behind any of them. Every buy needs an entry, a stop and a risk amount first.
wrong.Add names so you miss nothing: More names means less attention on each one. Narrowing is what lets you act fast when one sets up.

questions.story: Your plan: buy over $50, stop at $48. Overnight news hits. At 9:00 a.m. the stock is $53.50 premarket.
questions.q: If you buy at $53.50, what's your risk per share to the $48 stop?
choices: $5.50, up from $2
Still $2, the stop didn't move
$3.50, how far it gapped past $50
Less, the move is in my favor
questions.why: $5.50, up from $2. Risk per share is entry minus stop. The stop stayed at $48, but buying at $53.50 makes each share risk far more than your plan did.
questions.lesson_line: A gap rewrites your plan's numbers. Re-plan it or pass, but don't buy on the old math.

wrong.Still $2, the stop didn't move: The stop didn't move, but your entry did. Entry minus stop is now much wider.
wrong.$3.50, how far it gapped past $50: That's how far it ran past your $50 trigger, not the distance down to your stop.
wrong.Less, the move is in my favor: Paying more for the same stop means more risk per share, not less.

questions.q: It's 12:30 p.m. and the market has gone quiet. What comes first in your midday check?
choices: Positions, stops and news due later
A fresh scan for new names to buy
Lower stops to give trades more room
questions.answer: Positions, stops and news due later
questions.why: Positions, stops and news due later. Protection comes before new buys. Know what's scheduled too: the Fed's Oct. 28, 2026 statement landed at 2:00 p.m. ET.
questions.lesson_line: Midday is a check, not a hunt.

wrong.A fresh scan for new names to buy: New buys can wait. Veteran trader Gatis Roze checks what he owns first: protection takes precedence over fresh purchases.
wrong.Lower stops to give trades more room: Moving a stop lower on a long adds risk you never planned. Stops move with a trade, not away from it.

questions.story: At 2:00 p.m. the market whips both ways, and your stock swings through your stop and back. Later you learn the Fed's statement came out at 2:00.
questions.q: Which premarket step would have warned you?
choices: Checking the day's economic calendar
Reading the overnight index futures
Marking levels on each of your names
Scanning your names' news
questions.why: Checking the day's economic calendar. Rate announcements are on it, and the Fed's Oct. 28, 2026 statement came out at 2:00 p.m. ET. Big news like that can upset the day's normal rhythm.
questions.lesson_line: Levels tell you where. The calendar tells you when.

wrong.Reading the overnight index futures: Futures show the overnight mood. They don't tell you what's scheduled at 2:00 p.m.
wrong.Marking levels on each of your names: Levels tell you where to act, not when the market is about to jolt.
wrong.Scanning your names' news: Company news matters, but a Fed statement is market-wide and scheduled. It sits on the economic calendar.

questions.story: After the close you run your recap. One holding just made a new higher low, well above your stop.
questions.q: What does the recap do with that stop?
choices: Consider raising it under the new low
Lower it to give the trade more room
Cancel it, since the trade is working
questions.answer: Consider raising it under the new low
questions.why: Consider raising it under the new low. Schwab's daily routine: monitor open positions for new support levels and chances to adjust your stops. Support is usually a previous low.
questions.lesson_line: Stops move one way: in the direction of the trade.

wrong.Lower it to give the trade more room: Widening a stop on a winner adds risk for no reason.
wrong.Cancel it, since the trade is working: Working trades can turn. Without a stop, a winner can become a loser.

questions.story: You work 9 to 5 and can't watch the market. You hold two swing trades with stops planned at yesterday's lows.
questions.q: Where should those stops live during the day?
choices: As stop orders at your broker
In your head, checked at lunch
Nowhere until you get home
questions.answer: As stop orders at your broker
questions.why: As stop orders at your broker. Schwab notes stop orders can help protect you, especially when you can't watch your positions. Gatis Roze uses mental stops because he watches the market closely. A gap can still skip a stop.
questions.lesson_line: If you can't watch, your stops have to be real orders, not intentions.

wrong.In your head, checked at lunch: Between checks, nothing acts on it. A mental stop only works for someone watching the screen.
wrong.Nowhere until you get home: Then a bad day has no limit until you're home. That's a loss you never planned.

questions.story: You skipped Monday's recap and Tuesday's prep. At 4:05 p.m. Tuesday, a stock you hold reports. It falls 11% after hours.
questions.q: Which step would have flagged it in time?
choices: Checking earnings dates for holdings
Reading the futures each morning
Placing a stop under yesterday's low
The midday check on volume
questions.why: Checking earnings dates for holdings. Companies usually report before the open or after the close, and Schwab's routine checks the week ahead for earnings. Knowing it Monday gave you Tuesday's session to decide.
questions.lesson_line: Every day, check who reports tonight and tomorrow morning. Decide before the close, not after the gap.

wrong.Reading the futures each morning: Futures show the market's mood. They don't list a company's report date.
wrong.Placing a stop under yesterday's low: A stop can't stop a report. The stock can gap past it, and the fill lands far below.
wrong.The midday check on volume: Volume says nothing about a report date. The earnings calendar does.

questions.q: If you can't spend two hours on premarket prep, a routine isn't worth having.
questions.why: False. Build the routine around the day you really have. A good routine packs a lot of information into a short window.
questions.lesson_line: A short routine you run every day beats a long one you skip.

questions.story: For three weeks the S&P 500 has made lower highs and lower lows. Most names on your list broke support. One chart still looks perfect.
questions.q: How does your premarket treat that one name?
choices: Extra caution, the market is against it
Full size, a great chart is all you need
Buy the names that broke, they're cheap
questions.answer: Extra caution, the market is against it
questions.why: Extra caution. You do better trading in the direction of the bigger trend, and even strong stocks can drop fast when the market turns.
questions.lesson_line: Check the market before the stock. A great chart can still fail when the market falls.

wrong.Full size, a great chart is all you need: CAN SLIM checks market direction daily for a reason: even strong stocks can drop fast when the market turns.
wrong.Buy the names that broke, they're cheap: Broken support isn't a discount. It usually brings selling on the way back up.

questions.q: Written checklists are for beginners. Experienced traders run their routine from memory.
questions.why: False. Gatis Roze, trading his own account since 1989, works from written checklists and says to keep them in sight. SMB's Steve Spencer keeps a set list for his morning.
questions.lesson_line: Out of sight is out of mind. Write the routine down and keep it where you can see it.

questions.story: Down day. You took two small losses, both by the plan, and still hold three names. It's 4:10 p.m., and you want to shut the laptop and forget it.
questions.q: What does tonight's recap still need?
choices: Stops, reports due, tomorrow's list
Nothing, a red day earns a night off
A bigger list to win it back tomorrow
Looser stops so they don't hit again
questions.why: Stops, reports due, tomorrow's list. The recap isn't a mood check. It sets up tomorrow: stops reviewed, reports known, the next plan written while the market is closed.
questions.lesson_line: Red day or green day, the recap runs. It's how tomorrow starts.

wrong.Nothing, a red day earns a night off: Losses taken by the plan are the cost of trading. What you still hold and tomorrow's plan still need the recap.
wrong.A bigger list to win it back tomorrow: That's trading more to win back a loss. Investopedia calls revenge trading a recipe for disaster.
wrong.Looser stops so they don't hit again: Widening stops to dodge losses just makes the next loss bigger.

questions.story: You work days. You get 20 minutes before work and about an hour after 5 p.m.
questions.q: Where does the heavy planning go?
choices: Evenings: list, levels and stops
Mornings: scan everything from scratch
Lunch break: scan and buy midday
Skip prep and react to the open
questions.why: Evenings: list, levels and stops. That's your longest window, and the market is closed. Then the 20 morning minutes go to futures, the calendar and news on your names.
questions.lesson_line: Build the plan at night. Use the morning to check it, not to write it.

wrong.Mornings: scan everything from scratch: There's no time for that. Twenty minutes is for checking the plan, not building it.
wrong.Lunch break: scan and buy midday: Midday is for checking what you hold. Building the plan belongs to the hours when the market is closed.
wrong.Skip prep and react to the open: Then every decision is made on impulse, at the busiest, most volatile time of day.

conflicts: Premarket start time: Investopedia (s13) says premarket trading runs from 4 a.m. ET; FINRA (s6) says it is 'typically defined as taking place from 7 - 9:30 a.m. ET'; brokers differ. The unit never keys a premarket start time (F1.05 owns session hours).

No single order for the premarket: Steenbarger (s40) starts with overseas markets, the day's economic reports, yesterday's indicators and overnight Globex; Roze (s35, s32) starts with the news, the Nasdaq premarket pages and overseas markets, then runs top-down (market trends, then sectors, then stocks); Spencer (s41) runs platforms, his game plan, alerts, a scanner and his journal. Investopedia's 10 Steps (s17) looks at the stock first and then steps back to the market, the reverse of Roze's top-down. So no question keys a fixed order of steps. The unit keys only what they share: plan when the market is closed (q06, q22), know the calendar (q04, q08, q14), narrow the list (q11), set levels, stops and alerts (q05, q10), and read the market as well as the stock (q07, q19). The row's 'P: order the routine' is taught that way.

Steenbarger (t2) modifies his game plan as the morning reports come out, while Investopedia (it1) and Fidelity (fp1) say the plan's rules should not change while you are trading. Not a contradiction: Steenbarger adjusts his read of the market; the entry and stop rules stay. q06 keys the rules; q08 keys adjusting the plan to the report.

Trading the open: Investopedia's beginner day-trading guide (s16) suggests novices watch the first 15-20 minutes, and Roze (s35) is 'seldom active' in the first hour, while Investopedia's timing piece (s14) says many professionals focus on the opening hour. The unit never keys whether to trade the open.

Mental vs hard stops: Roze (rf2) uses 'soft' (mental) stops because he watches all session. q16 keys only the case of a member who cannot watch (a resting stop order), with Schwab (sb5) and the gap caveat (ips2); it does not say mental stops are wrong for someone at the screen.

Roze's StockCharts articles date from 2012-2013. They are cited only for process advice that does not expire (write routines down, fit them to your day, plan when the market is closed, check the group). His lunchtime 'manipulation' view and the Trader's Almanac last-half-hour statistic in the same series are not used.

Investopedia's economic-calendar page (s19) suggests a trader who 'guesses correctly' can open a position right before an announcement. That is a gamble on an unseen number, and the unit teaches the opposite (q08 wrong choice 'Buy all three before it comes out'); only the page's definition of the calendar (ie1) is cited.

Futures hours: Investopedia's E-mini page gives Sunday-Friday 6 p.m. to 5 p.m. ET with a 5-6 p.m. halt, but CME's own contract-spec table loads by script and could not be read as page text. The unit says only 'nearly 24 hours' (CME's own product page, fc1) and never keys exact futures hours.

Unit plan row 'covers': course M6 'premarket routine' and dossier M12 are docs/curriculum, which the contract forbids as a source; not used. The Journal day-notes shape (prep, mid-day, recap) matches the unit's three checkpoints, but no house page states a routine in the owner's words, so the only house question (q10) rests on the owner's default stop (sizing_rule.md section 2), which F9.02 also asks directly; q10 asks it from the premarket angle (before the open only yesterday's low exists).

Overlap with F8.07 (the daily MENTAL routine, same Steenbarger morning posts): F8.07 owns the warm-up of the trader, breaks and the emotional cool-down; this unit owns the market and process side (futures, calendar, list, levels, alerts, midday check, the mechanical recap). Facts shared with F8.07 (Spencer's morning list, Steenbarger's game plan) are asked here from a different angle. Overlap with F7.07 (release times), F5.04 (earnings timing) and F1.05 / F10.04 (extended hours): those facts appear here only inside routine decisions, never asked as the same recall question.
